{"url": "https://export.arxiv.org/api/query?search_query=all%3AHow+do+episodic+memory+recall+mechanisms+in+reinforcement+learning+influence+long-term+preference+stability+and+path-dependent+behavior%3F&max_results=4", "scope": "paper abstracts; preprints, peer-review status not verified", "excerpt": "title: Memory-Efficient Episodic Control Reinforcement Learning with Dynamic Online k-means
id: http://arxiv.org/abs/1911.09560v1
published: 2019-11-21T15:54:49Z
summary: Recently, neuro-inspired episodic control (EC) methods have been developed to overcome the data-inefficiency of standard deep reinforcement learning approaches. Using non-/semi-parametric models to estimate the value function, they learn rapidly, retrieving cached values from similar past states. In realistic scenarios, with limited resources and noisy data, maintaining meaningful representations in memory is essential to speed up the learning and avoid catastrophic forgetting. Unfortunately, EC methods have a large space and time complexity. We investigate different solutions to these problems based on prioritising and ranking stored states, as well as online clustering techniques. We also propose a new dynamic online k-means algorithm that is both computationally-efficient and yields significantly better performance at smaller memory sizes; we validate this approach on classic reinforcement learning environments and Atari games.

title: Carousel Memory: Rethinking the Design of Episodic Memory for Continual Learning
id: http://arxiv.org/abs/2110.07276v3
published: 2021-10-14T11:27:45Z
summary: Continual Learning (CL) is an emerging machine learning paradigm that aims to learn from a continuous stream of tasks without forgetting knowledge learned from the previous tasks. To avoid performance decrease caused by forgetting, prior studies exploit episodic memory (EM), which stores a subset of the past observed samples while learning from new non-i.i.d. data. Despite the promising results, since CL is often assumed to execute on mobile or IoT devices, the EM size is bounded by the small hardware memory capacity and makes it infeasible to meet the accuracy requirements for real-world applications. This paper examines why company law, securities regulation and governance codes do not always prevent board capture, minority shareholder abuse, related-party transaction misuse and disclosure failure in African emerging markets. It adopts a structured doctrinal and comparative corporate governance review, supported by selected case analysis from Nigeria, Kenya, South Africa and Ghana. The paper develops a Legal Accountability Gap framework to show how governance failure occurs when formal duties are weakened by concentrated ownership, weak regulatory capacity, costly litigation, political connections, audit market limitations and limited investor enforcement. The analysis shows that the central problem is not simply the absence of corporate governance rules, but the gap between legal design and institutional consequence. South Africa demonstrates that sophisticated governance codes can still fail where audit, board and market accountability are weak. Nigeria and Kenya show how insider lending, related-party abuse and disclosure failure can destabilise firms and financial systems.
